🐛 Bug
Permuting more than two axes of a Tensor before feeding it to a checkpointed Conv2d layer causes a crash during the backward pass when CUDA is enabled. All three conditions appear to be necessary: if exactly 2 axes are permuted, if the first layer in the checkpoint is not specifically of type torch.nn.Conv2d, or if the operations are performed on CPU, no error occurs.
To Reproduce
Here's some (fairly) minimal reproduction code, tested on my Ubuntu machine and on Google Colab. It crashes iff CUDA is available:
import torch
from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint

class ConvModel(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_in):
        super(ConvModel, self).__init__()
        self.init = torch.nn.Conv2d(n_in, n_in, 1)
        self.conv = torch.nn.Conv2d(n_in, n_in, 1)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x.permute(0, 3, 1, 2)
        x = self.init(x) # natural way to enable x.requires_grad before the checkpoint
        x = checkpoint(self.conv, x)
        return x


# Some constants
batch_size = 1
n_in = 10
h_w = 10

cuda = torch.cuda.is_available()

m = ConvModel(n_in)
if(cuda):
    m = m.cuda()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(m.parameters())
loss_fn = torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

# Simple training loop; nothing fancy here
for i in range(1000):
    optimizer.zero_grad()

    # Arbitrary inputs
    inp = torch.rand((batch_size, h_w, h_w, n_in))
    target = torch.zeros((batch_size, h_w, h_w), dtype=torch.int64)
    if(cuda):
        inp = inp.cuda()
        target = target.cuda()

    out = m(inp)
    loss = loss_fn(out, target)
    loss.backward() # crash occurs here
    optimizer.step()

Note that the input to the checkpoint is passed through an initial convolutional layer. This has the effect of enabling requires_grad for x. This is a prerequisite for at least one of the inputs to each checkpoint (see e.g. this thread).

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Bug
In Python, isinstance can be used with a single element or a tuple of elements. torch.jit.isinstance doesn't consider the case that we want to compare against a tuple of elements.
Example
import torch
from typing import List

def fn(x: int):
    if torch.jit.isinstance(x, (List[str], str)):
        z = x + "bar"
        return z
    else:
        return "baz"
The above example errors out with:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test/tinytest.py", line 11, in <module>
    print(fn(1))
  File "test/tinytest.py", line 5, in fn
    if torch.jit.isinstance(x, (List[str], str)):
  File "/home/ansley/local/miniconda3/envs/pytorch/lib/python3.8/site-packages/torch/jit/__init__.py", line 185, in isinstance
    return _isinstance(obj, target_type)
  File "/home/ansley/local/miniconda3/envs/pytorch/lib/python3.8/site-packages/torch/_jit_internal.py", line 1145, in _isinstance
    return isinstance(obj, target_type)
  File "/home/ansley/local/miniconda3/envs/pytorch/lib/python3.8/typing.py", line 769, in __instancecheck__
    return self.__subclasscheck__(type(obj))
  File "/home/ansley/local/miniconda3/envs/pytorch/lib/python3.8/typing.py", line 777, in __subclasscheck__
    raise TypeError("Subscripted generics cannot be used with"
TypeError: Subscripted generics cannot be used with class and instance checks

Note that this is only a problem in eager (Python) mode. If you run it in script (torch.jit.script) mode, it will be fine.
Notes
This would be a nice introduction to the PyTorch codebase. I'm writing notes here with the idea that this would be an OSS project or a Bootcamp task.
Our implementation of torch.jit.isinstance is at torch/_jit_internal.py:_isinstance. In _isinstance, if target_type is a tuple literal, the logic falls through to the line return isinstance(obj, target_type), which fails for "subscripted generics". A "subscripted generic" is a type annotation that has other types inside it, e.g. List[int], Dict[str, int], Optional[int]. (Some examples of types that are NOT subscripted generics are int, str, etc.)
What we want to do is: Check if current element is a tuple literal containing types. If we do have a tuple literal, try calling _isinstance on all types in the tuple. If any of the elements in the tuple are subtypes of the current element, return true, else return false.
I haven't coded this up myself. If my suggested algorithm breaks everything and you want to yell at me, reach out at ansley@fb.com

🐛 Bug
The calculation of the second moment estimate for Adam (torch.optim.Adam) assumes that the parameters being optimized over are real-valued. This leads to unexpected behavior when using Adam to optimize over complex-valued parameters. AdamW, Adadelta, and potentially other Adam-related optimizers are affected as well.
The issue is that variance is currently estimated from param.grad * param.grad, but for complex numbers the appropriate calculation is param.grad * param.grad.conj(), a.k.a. t.abs(param.grad * param.grad). As currently implemented, the variance estimate is complex-valued, which causes unexpected behavior and prevents convergence in almost all cases when optimizing over complex parameters. The properly calculated variance remains real-valued, even for complex-valued parameters, and behaves as expected across both real and complex-valued parameters. The original source noting this issue and the fix, as far as I am aware, is Andy Saroff's Dissertation.
To Reproduce
The following script demonstrates a simple optimization problem where the as-implemented version of Adam fails:
import torch as t
from matplotlib import pyplot as plt

complex_param = t.tensor([1],dtype=t.complex64, requires_grad=True)

# We will optimize on the mean squared error from a 1j
target = 1j

def calc_loss(x):
    return t.abs(x - target)**2

optimizer = t.optim.Adam([complex_param], lr=0.001)

n = 10000
values = t.zeros(n, dtype=t.complex64)
for i in range(n):
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss = calc_loss(complex_param)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    values[i] = complex_param.detach()


# Plot the results
plt.plot(values.real, label='Real Part')
plt.plot(values.imag, label='Imaginary Part')
plt.legend()
plt.xlabel('Iteration')
plt.ylabel('Complex Parameter')
plt.title('Optimization Progress with as-implemented Adam')
plt.show()
This script produces the following plot:

Expected behavior

Allow the input argument params to ZeroRedundancyOptimizer be an iterable of dicts.

In the normal Optimizer implementation, the input argument params can be either an iterable of torch.Tensors or an iterable of dicts (see here). 🚀 Feature

Implement heterogeneous  parameterdtype support in ZeroRedundancyOptimizer.
Motivation

DDP supports model parameters and hence gradients having varying dtype, as seen in the bucket assignment implementation. Currently, the ZeroRedundancyOptimizer implementation assumes that all parameters have the same dtype when parameters_as_bucket_view is set to True. To follow in the generality of DDP, the ZeRO implementation should remove this assumption.
Pitch

Right now, the buffer size for a bucket is computed by the number of participating elements times the size of the first parameter, assuming a uniform size for all parameters in the bucket. Instead, a more sophisticated bucketing algorithm is needed to accommodate varying parameter dtypes (e.g. sparse versus dense tensors, different precisions, float versus integer, etc.). Note that sparse vectors pose a unique challenge since their space requirement is variable.

This is best illustrated with an example:

class Model(nn.Module):

model = Model()
model.linear.register_buffer('mask', torch.ones(model.linear.weight.shape))

class WeightMaskParametrization(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, layer):
        super().__init__()
        self.layer = layer
        
    def forward(self, w):

print(model)  # <- this will throw a recursion error

class WeightMaskParametrization(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, mask):
        super().__init__()
        self.mask = mask
        
    def forward(self, w):
        return self.mask * w

weight_mask = WeightMaskParametrization(model.linear.mask)
parametrize.register_parametrization(model.linear, 'weight', weight_mask)

weight_mask = WeightMaskParametrization(model.linear.mask)
parametrize.register_parametrization(model.linear, 'weight', weight_mask)
model.linear.mask = torch.zeros(model.linear.weight.shape)

🚀 Feature
Lazy modules (i.e. module that inherits from torch.nn.modules.lazy.LazyModuleMixin) should accept keyword arguments to forward method, to have API syntax parity with non-lazy modules.
Motivation
If we have a non-lazy module with keyword argument:
import torch

class MyNonLazyModule(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.c = 100
    def forward(self, a, b=1):
        return a + b + self.c
We can pass keyword argument when calling this module:
m = MyNonLazyModule()

m(1, b=2)  # gives 103
m(a=1)  # gives 102
m(a=1, b=2)  # gives 103
But if we have a lazy module with keyword argument:
import torch

class MyLazyModule(torch.nn.modules.lazy.LazyModuleMixin, torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.c = 100
    def initialize_parameters(self, a, b=1):
        if b == 1:
            self.c = 100
        else:
            self.c = 200
    def forward(self, a, b=1):
        return a + b + self.c
Passing keyword argument when calling this module would either have incorrect behavior or just fail:
m = MyLazyModule()

m(1, b=2)  # gives 103, but it should be 203 if we strictly follow the `initialize_parameters` logic.
m(a=1)  # fails with "TypeError: initialize_parameters() missing 1 required positional argument: 'a'".
m(a=1, b=2)  # fails with "TypeError: initialize_parameters() missing 1 required positional argument: 'a'".
Pitch
Lazy modules (i.e. module that inherits from torch.nn.modules.lazy.LazyModuleMixin) should accept kwargs to forward method, to have API syntax parity with non-lazy modules.
The current implementation of LazyModuleMixin uses forward pre-hook. Forward pre-hook doens't accept kwargs now, but we can consider changing it:
# in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/095cd6a0da255a5ed24d146898c53790f0e9c3f0/torch/nn/modules/module.py#L1063
...
- result = hook(self, input)

+ if len(inspect.signature(hook).parameters) == 3:
+    result = hook(self, input, kwargs)
+ else:
+    result = hook(self, input)
...
to make it accept kwargs without breaking BC for all existing hooks.
Alternatives
An alternative is forking LazyModuleMixin and adding support for accepting kwargs to forward pre-hooks and _infer_parameters. But it would be great to not need to fork because there will be a lot more code to maintain.
Additional context
Lazy module is very common in FB-internal RecSys ecosystem. Almost all DPER modules are "lazy module", and as we build out the PyTorch-based RecSys ecosystem internally, we would like to provide the same API syntax for lazy modules as non-lazy modules, to make sure internal users can fully enjoy the UX advantage of PyTorch.

🚀 Feature

In this doc we are requesting comments for the implementation of the sparsification flow as part of architecture optimization namespace (torch.ao)
with: @raghuramank100 @dskhudia @kimishpatel @kazhou
Motivation
We present a workflow for training/preparing sparse models and mapping them into efficient kernels for fast inference. This workflow aims to be flexible (i.e you can customize how you want to train a sparse model) and composable (sparsity can plug and play with existing training and with quantization). We are looking for feedback on

Is this workflow suitable for your needs?
Is this sufficient for creating sparse and quantized models?
Are the operators that we plan to support a good match for what you need?

This document describes the flow for the fast inference using sparse kernels in pytorch. This is motivated by:

Sparsity is a well known technique that can provide significant speedup during inference on server, mobile and GPUs (A100) with kernels optimized for sparsity.
Tensorflow supports sparsity: TF training support, with sparse fp32 and quantized inference support for mobile in TFLite
Custom hardware support for sparsity is expanding.
Internal experiments on NLP and recommendation models show the benefits of sparsity for faster inference, with kernel level speedups of up to 2x on mobile devices with 75% sparsity. For actual models, the speedups observed are on the order of 20%.

Goals
The main purpose of this document is to describe the workflow for users to be able to train models with weight sparsity and obtain fast inference with optimized kernels. Specifically, we will describe:

User facing APIs supporting end to end workflow for training and inference with sparse models.
APIs and kernels for faster inference and compressed model sizes.
Integration of sparsity with pytorch stack

Note that while the training APIs for sparsity are general and support flexible sparsity patterns for weights, the inference kernels are optimized for specific block sparsity patterns.
Sparsity Stack Overview

Vertically, the sparsity framework is split into python and c++. Most of the Python code is user-facing API, while the C++ code the kernels and ops.  Note that currently, sparse operations specified here are supported only for sparse weights and dense activations. We do not support sparse activations.
User Facing APIs
There are three user facing APIs for sparsity:

torch.ao.sparsity -- model transformation utilities

torch.ao.sparsity.sparsifier -- Primary class for model transformation
torch.ao.sparsity.scheduler -- Class for modifying the Sparsifier configuration during training


torch.ao.nn.sparse -- subclasses of nn.Module[Support sparse inference]

Linear -- Sparse Weights and Dense Activations, all in fp32
ConvXd -- TBD


torch.ao.nn.sparse.quantized

Linear -- Sparse and quantized weights with quantized activations
ConvXd


torch.ao.nn.sparsity -- subclasses of nn.Module[Support sparsity workflow]

fakeSparse -- Fake sparsity module for modeling sparsity during training


torch.ao.nn.sparse.functional -- stateless implementations of the sparse layers

Sparsifier Design
In the simplest case, invoking sparsity is as simple as:
Model = myModelClass()
sparsity_config = [{'module' :...}, {'module' :...}]

# Create the sparsifier and specify which modules get sparsified
sparsifier = TheSparsifierClass(sparsity_config)
# Prepare the model, insert fake-sparse ops for training
sparsifier.prepare(model)
def train_one_epoch(...):
    for input, target in dataset:
       optimizer.zero_grad()
       output = model(input)
       loss = loss_fn(output, target)
       loss.backward()
       optimizer.step()
       # Update masks
       sparsifier.step()

for epoch in range(num_epochs):
   train_one_epoch()

# Finally, when training is done, convert for inference with sparse kernels
sparsifier.convert(model)
Broadly, the design for sparsity follows the implementation of optimizers in pytorch. This is because:

Sparsity operates only on weights of a model, just like optimizers.
In contrast to quantization, sparsity mask calculation may not be local. Having a single sparsifier object allows for global information to be used for sparsity mask calculation.
Sparsity mask computation can depend on both gradients and weights.

Sparsifier Requirements

Composable support for sparsity: Models can be sparsified with or without quantization.
Configurable support: Granularity of sparsity, sparsity level, metrics to determine how weights are sparsified needs to be user configurable with good defaults
Training-Aware/Post Training support: Sparsity needs to be supported for both post training and training modes, with the expectation that training is typically needed for acceptable accuracy tradeoff.
Local/Global Sparsity Support: The level of sparsity in a tensor can depend on local statistics (i.e the tensor itself or activations that operate on the tensor) or global statistics (tensors anywhere in the network) or gradients.
Eager and FX support: Support for sparsity in both eager and FX workflows.

Design Choices
There are multiple design choices that a user faces during the sparsity studies. As a platform, we will provide support for the following options



Option
Supported Design Choices




Sparsity Granularity (Training)
Arbitrary2:4 structured-sparse


Sparsity Granularity (Inference)
1x4 for x86 CPU1x4, 8x1 for mobile2:4 structured-sparse for GPU (s.a. NVidia A100 sparsity)


Sparse Matrix Update Scheme
In-placeNon in-place (Out of place)


Sparsification Scope
LocalGlobal


Tensors used for mask calculation
WeightsGradientsActivations*



* The sparsification targets are always the weights, meaning during the inference only the weights are sparsified.
In addition to the options above, we support the sparsity scheduler, which makes sure the sparsity mask updates/calculations are flexible.
Granularity

Granularity of sparsity (block size) is dictated mainly by the underlying hardware on which inference is performed. Our goal is to make this completely flexible for training. For inference we plan to support:

1 x 4 [out features/channels, in features/channels] for x86 CPU. Any multiple of 1 x 4 in either or both dimensions, for example, 2 x 4 or 1 x 8 or 2 x 8, will also work.
8x1 for ARM CPU


For the NVidia Sparsity support, granularity m:n means “m out of n elements in a tensor row are set to zero”. Specifically for A100 devices, it is 2 out 4.

Sparse Matrix Update


In-place option updates the sparse tensor by performing , where   is the tensor to be updated, and the  is the sparsity mask. Once the tensor  is updated, the sparse values are zeroed-out.

Pros: Requires only one copy of the sparse tensor to be stored (+ mask)
Cons: Once a mask is applied to a weight, it is zeroed out, all past history is lost. These weights cannot regrow.



Non in-place updates don't modify the tensor directly, but perform the following:



Pros: The original tensor is preserved (the masked elements are not updated via backprop). Weights can regrow if the mask changes.
Cons: In addition to the unmasked weights (W), the masked weights (W’) are computed and resident in memory for forward/backward computations.



Sparsification Scope
The sparsification scope identifies the scope in which the mask is computed.

Local scope implies that the sparsity mask is only computed with respect to the layer statistics.

Pros: Simple mask computing
Cons: Potentially sub-optimal accuracy vs sparsity tradeoff.


Global scope means that the sparsity statistics are not bounded by a single layer, but can span over multiple layers if needed.

Pros: No need for per-layer thresholds. The tensor statistics is shared across layers, and normalization is used across layers to allow for it.
Cons: Increased complexity when computing the masks.



Tensors used for mask calculation
For sparsity, we need to compute an importance score for every connection, i.e weight in the model.

Weights:  Use weight magnitude as a metric to determine which weights can be sparsified. This method is the simplest for inference as the weight tensors are constant.
Gradients: Compute importance based on both weights and gradient norms.
Activations: In some research papers, the norm of the activations that are applied with the weight of interest are used to compute the importance score.

For all training workflows, users can invoke sparsity and control mask calculation at different epochs.
How to use a sparsifier
To use torch.ao.sparsity you have to construct a sparsifier object that will hold the current state and will update the mask and the parameters (weights).
Constructing
To construct a sparsifier you have to give it the parameters that will be sparsified. You also might want to give it the sparsification parameters, such as block pattern, update scheme, etc.
For example, the simplest way to use a sparsifier is shown below. Note: TheSparsifierClass is just an example name. See the "Algorithms" section for real sparsifiers.
# Use the sparsifier with the predefined config
sparsity_config = [
  {'module': model.linear1, 'sparsity_level': 0.8, 'sparsity_pattern': [1, 4], 'zeros_per_block': 4, 'inplace': True},
  {'module': model.linear2, 'sparsity_level': 0.7, 'sparsity_pattern': [2, 4], 'zeros_per_block': 4, 'inplace': True},
]
sparsifier = TheSparsifierClass(sparsity_config)
# Use the sparsifier with default arguments
sparsity_config = [
  {'module': model.linear1, 'sparsity_level': 0.8, 'sparsity_pattern': [1, 4], 'zeros_per_block': 4, 'inplace': True},
  {'module': model.linear2},
]
sparsifier = TheSparsifierClass(sparsity_config, sparsity_level=0.7, sparsity_pattern=[2, 4], zeros_per_block=4, inplace=True)
The exact arguments for the sparsifier will be defined by specific implementation of the different sparsifiers. The arguments in the example above would represent the following:

sparsity_level: Target level of sparsity that needs to be achieved.
sparsity_pattern: The shape of the sparse block
zeros_per_block: Number of zeros per sparse block.
inplace: Inplace weight updates, without saving an auxiliary data structure for the mask

Sparsifier Config
The configuration of the sparsifier is provided as a list, with each element representing the configuration for a specific module. The elements in the list could be:

torch module (instance of torch layer): The sparsification arguments will be inferred from the default arguments
Dict: This might include the sparsification parameters that apply to this module only. Note: the dicts MUST have a ‘module’ key that map to the layer that will be sparsified.

sparsity_config = [
    model.linear1,               # Will use default sparsity parameters
    model.linear2,               # Will use default sparsity parameters
    {'module': model.linear3},   # Will use default sparsity parameters
    {'module': model.linear4,
     'sparsity_level': 0.9,
     'sparsity_pattern': [1, 4],
     'zeros_per_block': 4},
]
sparsifier = TheSparsifierClass(sparsity_config,
                                sparsity_level=0.7,
                                sparsity_pattern=(1, 8),
                                zeros_per_block=4)
Preparing a model
The first step for sparsifying the model is to insert operations for masking the weights of the model. This is done by the prepare step.
If the sparsifier implementation requires keeping the unmasked weights, masked weights are computed from the original weights and the mask. If not, the weights are used as is without any modifications. After this step the forward and backward passes include the effect of sparsity in computations.
model = TheModelClass()
sparsifier = TheSparsifierClass(sparsity_config, sparsity_level=0.99) # Change this part
sparsifier.prepare(model)
optimizer = TheOptimizerClass(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
for input, target in dataset:
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    output = model(input)
    loss = loss_fn(output, target)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    sparsifier.step()
Taking a sparsification step
All sparsifiers implement a step() method that updates the mask with the logic being determined by the sparsifier implementation. The step method does the following:

Computes the mask for the weights
If the weights are updated in-place, i.e the masked elements of the weight matrix are zeroed out, this method also applies the mask to the weights.

optimizer = TheOptimizerClass(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
sparsifier = TheSparsifierClass(sparsity_config, sparsity_level=0.99)
for input, target in dataset:
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    output = model(input)
    loss = loss_fn(output, target)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    sparsifier.step()
NOTE: The optimizer step() method has to be called before the sparsifier step(). This ensures that in-case weights are updated in-place, masked weights do not re-grow due to gradient accumulation.
Converting the model
The model conversion is the last step, and is done using the sparsifier instance.
from torch.ao.sparsity import convert
sparse_model = sparsifier.convert(model)
Convert replaces the floating point operators with the sparsified operators. In addition, convert applies the mask to the dense weights and packs them as required by sparse kernels for efficient inference. Note that depending on the sparsity level, convert can choose to use dense kernels if no speedup is expected.
Saving/Loading a sparsifier
The sparsifier can be saved and loaded using the state_dict. Analogous to optimizers, sparsifier state dict only contains parameters relevant to the sparsifier. Weights and masks are part of the model and are stored as part of the model state dict.
Notice that because the model.linear2 had the parameters set explicitly, we also save the parameters separately.
To save/load the sparsifier you can use torch.save and torch.load:
torch.save({
    'epoch': epoch,
    'model_state_dict': model.state_dict(),
    'optimizer_state_dict': optimizer.state_dict(),
    'sparsifier_state_dict': sparsifier.state_dict(),
    'loss': loss,
    ...}, PATH)

model = TheModelClass(*args, **kwargs)
optimizer = TheOptimizerClass(*args, **kwargs)
sparsifier = TheSparsifierClass(*args, **kwargs)

checkpoint = torch.load(PATH)
model.load_state_dict(checkpoint['model_state_dict'])
optimizer.load_state_dict(checkpoint['optimizer_state_dict'])
sparsifier.load_state_dict(checkpoint['sparsifier_state_dict'])
epoch = checkpoint['epoch']
loss = checkpoint['loss']
Writing your own sparsifier
To write a custom sparsifier one could inherit from the BaseSparsifier and implement some of the methods. For example, if implementing a sparsifier that computes the mask depending on some predefined threshold:
class HardThresholdSparsifier(torch.ao.sparsity.Sparsifier):
    def __init__(self, threshold, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.threshold = threshold

    def update_mask(self, group):
        mask = group['mask']
        weight = group['param']
        mask[weight < self.threshold] = 0
        group['mask'] = mask

    def step(self):
        if self.enable_mask_update:
            for group in self.module_groups:
                self.update_mask(group)
        super().step()
It is the responsibility of the base class to call the self.update_mask when appropriate.
Scheduler
The sparsity scheduler is used to control the update of the sparsification parameters. The scheduler would control:

Sparsity threshold levels
Frequency of mask calculation
Frequency of mask update to weights

For example
optimizer = TheOptimizerClass(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
sparsifier = TheSparsifierClass(per_module_config)
sp_scheduler = TheSchedulerClass(sparsifier, init_sr=0.1, goal_sr=0.99, last_epoch=-1)
lr_scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.StepLR(optimizer, ...)

for epoch in range(EPOCHS):
    for input, target in dataset:
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        output = model(input)
        loss = loss_fn(output, target)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        sparsifier.step()

    sp_scheduler.step()
    lr_scheduler.step()
Notice in the example above the sparsity level will be controlled by the scheduler.
Writing your own scheduler
To write a custom sparsity scheduler, one must inherit from the BaseScheduler, and implement the get_sl method
class LinearIncrementScheduler(torch.ao.sparsity.Scheduler):
    """Increments the level of sparsity until reached a max"""
    def __init__(self, increment, max_sparsity=1.0, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(self, *args, **kwargs)
        self.increment = increment
        self.max_sparsity = max_sparsity

        self.increment = [self.increment] * len(self.sparsifier.module_groups)
        self.sparsity_levels = self.base_sl

    def get_sl(self):
        super().step()  # Call this to increment counters. No scheduling is done in the base class
        for idx in range(len(self.increment)):
            self.sparsity_levels[idx] += self.increment
            self.sparsity_levels[idx] = min(self.sparsity_levels[idx], self.max_sparsity)
        return self.sparsity_levels
The example above shows the scheduler incrementing the level of sparsity at every call to the step. Notice that the only method that needs to be implemented is the get_sl which returns a list of floats representing the new level of sparsity.
Sparsity Workflows with Quantization
So far, we looked at sparsity in isolation.  Here we look at how the sparsity flow can be combined with the quantization. Refer to the examples below
Post Training Sparsity and Quantization
In this simplest case, the model is sparsified and quantized post training. Note that the sparsifier is first applied to the model. This is needed to ensure that the dynamic ranges for activations are estimated correctly for quantization. Also note that the convert method for the sparsifier will convert modules to the required kernels based on user configuration: sparse, sparse+quantized or quantized.
model.qconfig = tq.default_qconfig
sparsifier = TheSparsifierClass(per_module_config)
sparsifier.prepare(model)
# We want to call the sparsifier first, so that quantized model is calibrated correctly
sparsifier.step()

# Now we can prepare, calibrate, and convert
prep_model = tq.prepare(model)
prep_model(calibration_data)

# The sparsifier is aware of the quantization kernel, and decides which layers use what backend [Sparse/Quantized/Sparse + Quantized]
converted_model = sparsifier.convert(prep_model) 
QAT + Sparsity
Similarly, for quantization and sparsity aware training, we first insert fake-quants to model quantization during training. This is followed by the sparsifier prepare call, which inserts fake-sparse operators. The recommended sequence is to have fake-sparse operators precede fake-quantization operators and that is achieved by the sequence below:
sparsifier = TheSparsifierClass(per_module_config, target_ratio=0.1, block_pattern=[1, 4], local=True)
model = sparsifier.prepare(model)
model = tq.prepare_qat(model, qconfig_dict)
# Sparsifiers prepare function inserts fake-quant+fake-sparse operators to the weights
# Fake Quant + Fake Sparse operations are also fused.
for epoch in range(EPOCHS):
    for input, target in dataset:
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        output = model(input)
        loss = loss_fn(output, target)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        sparsifier.step()
# Similar to PTQ flow, a single call to convert is all that is needed.
sparsifier.convert(prep_model)
Backend
We plan to create ops in the separate name-spaces torch.ops.sparse and torch.ops.sparse_quantized. The operators here are not user facing and are accessed via modules.
We plan to start by supporting sparsity for server (x86) and mobile (ARM) CPU backends.  At a later point, we may support GPU inference too. We plan to support both fp32 sparsity and quantized sparsity kernels, with priority given to quantized sparse kernels as they provide the most speedup. This requires interfacing with three different backend libraries: QNNPACK (ARM, quantized), XNNPACK (ARM float), FBGEMM (x86- float and quantized)
Supported sparsity patterns
If there are multiple patterns that are supported, we should be able to dispatch based on the current level. Note that what is listed here is the smallest granularity of sparsity that is supported. Any multiple of the pattern size here will also work.



Pattern
FBGEMM (fp32)
FBGEMM (quantized)
QNNPACK (quantized)
XNNPACK (fp32)




1x1n

FBGEMM Sparsity Support
We have implemented sparse-matrix dense-matrix multiplication (SpMM) kernels for both 32-bit floating-point (FP32) data type and 8-bit integer (INT8) computation for serving pruned models efficiently on x86-64 CPUs in the FBGEMM library. For the tested matrix multiplication shapes, with an 80% sparsity in the weight matrix, the SpMM kernels can improve the computation performance by 1.087.06x and 1.7815.65x for FP32 and INT8, respectively. These shapes are gathered from various models used in production. An optimized INT8 sparse-matrix dense-vector multiplication (SpMV) is also implemented and achieves 1.62~3.10x speedup on the tested shapes.
SpMM and SpMV kernels both worked on packed weight data. Since weight is constant during inference, we can pack it once and use it multiple times thus allowing us to perform optimized compute. For packing the data, we use a variation on the popular sparse matrix format called Compressed Sparse Row (CSR). We use Tiled Block CSR format for packing the weight matrix. Main improvement over CSR is storing non-zero block indices instead of each non-zero element index and tiling in one of the matrix dimensions for efficient cpu cache use during computation.
Main restriction on sparsity granularity comes from the use of vector instruction VPMADDUBSW on current generation of processors (up to Skylake microarchitecture) and VPDPBUSDS instruction on recently released and upcoming generation of processors (Cascade Lake onwards) [8]. These instructions work on int8 data and do horizontal operations on the SIMD vectors in groups of 4. Hence, the restrictions on sparsity granularity to be 4 in input features dimension.
QNNPACK Sparsity support:
At the moment qnnpack support dynamically quantized sparse linear operator. Supported sparsity pattern is 8x1 and 1x4. Operator does weight prepacking in block CSR format much like FBGEMM. Expected activation format is batch x output_features. Internally, operator prepacks activation in custom format such that 8 rows of activations are transposed and packed together. Specific packing format, for 8x1 sparsity, is N/8,C/4,4c,8n, where N/n=batch dimension and C/c= output features dimension.
At 70% sparsity, for 1x4 sparsity we observed speedup of about 60% speedup. At same sparsity level for 8x1 pattern we observed about 3x speedup. Benchmarking was done for various shapes we had observed in the models of interest where batch size was relatively small.
Prioritization

Support for sparse kernels with static and dynamic quantization, no fp32 sparsity support.
Support for local sparsity first.
Support for sparsity with quantization aware training.

References

The State of Sparsity in Deep Neural Networks, Trevor Gale, Erich Elsen, Sara Hooker https://arxiv.org/pdf/1902.09574.pdf
What is the state of neural network pruning? Davis Blalock, Jose Javier Gonzalez Ortiz, Jonathan Frankle, John Guttag https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.03033
To prune, or not to prune: exploring the efficacy of pruning for model compression, Suyug Gupta, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.01878.pdf

clang-tidy is the last big missing piece of #55847, to enable it we need a way for devs to easily grab the specific version of clang-tidy we use in CI (with our custom checks and all). We could store these binaries in S3 for Linux / Mac once we have the build going and change make setup_lint to download and install them.
It'd also be nice for clang-tidy to be a statically built binary just so we can be sure that once downloaded onto the right OS/arch it can be run without issue (so long as the binary size is reasonable). LLVM builds clang-tidy dynamically by default and there doesn't seem to be a simple way to turn on a static build so this is something we'll have to figure out. Once that's done we can build statically in the clang-tidy Docker image and docker cp it out and upload to S3.

def weighted_mse(y, pred, x, mask, weight=10):

At the moment, when we have a non-contiguous matrix of batch of matrices, we instantiate a contiguous copy of it before passing it to BLAS. We can do better as BLAS / LAPACK have flags for the cases when a matrix is transposed / conjugate transposed (see here).
Given the recent work by @anjali411 on conjugate views, we do have a flag that is set whenever a tensor is conjugated. We could add a flag to is_contiguous or implement a new function is_fortran_contiguous (or is_column_major_contiguous? name under discussion).
After that, the plan would be to use all these tools to dispatch the correct flag to each BLAS routine. Note that all this handling would be transparent to the user. The user would just call matmul or @  and everything would be dispatched correctly automagically.
